_comment: The vocabulary and the taste of the video skill. Toolbay Stack, Copyright (c) 2026 Toolbay. MIT. Original work.
Everything a human would argue about lives in this file: which surfaces exist, how long a
video should be on each one, what aspect that surface is, which words in a prompt mean which
surface, what shots a launch video is made of, and the sentence the skill says when it
explains a decision. scripts/tb-video.mjs contains none of it. The code knows there is such
a thing as a platform and that a platform has a duration and a reason; it does not know that
Reels is 9:16, that 22 seconds is the cliff, or that the word 'ig' means Instagram.
This is the same split as skills/modes/modes.json and skills/memory/memory.json, and it is
here for the same reason: the thing most likely to be WRONG is a value, not a code path. When
22 seconds turns out to be 19, that is a one-line edit by whoever noticed, not a patch.
HOW MATCHING WORKS. Every 'match' array is a list of literal lowercase phrases. A prompt is
lowercased and searched for each phrase as a whole word (or as a substring when the phrase
already contains a space). Longer phrases score higher than short ones, so 'youtube shorts'
beats 'youtube'. Nothing here is a regular expression; if you can type it, you can add it.
Diffusion Studio's CLI. It is NOT on npm: @diffusionstudio/cli 404s on the registry, and
the only published packages are @diffusionstudio/core (the browser engine) and
@diffusionstudio/jsx (the types). dapi ships bundled inside the Diffusion Studio desktop
app, so getting the app is what puts the CLI within reach. The commands below are the ones
the editor's own README documents; the CLI is self-describing, so `dapi <group> --help` is
the authority if any of this drifts.
install: dapi is not on npm. It ships inside the Diffusion Studio app.
macOS, app already installed from the .dmg:
Diffusion Studio > Install dapi Command Line Tool
Any platform, from source (Node 20+ and npm):
cp apps/web/.env.example apps/web/.env      # the app will not run without it
npm run dev:desktop                          # builds the CLI and launches the app
The published download is macOS (Apple Silicon) only. On Windows the from-source path is
the only one, and it wants a running Electron app for the CLI to talk to.

_comment: What the finished file has to prove before this skill will call it a render. These are the
arguments handed to tb-video-evidence.mjs; the checks themselves are not configurable,
because a tolerance you can widen to infinity is not a check.
toleranceSeconds is half a second because encoders land a frame or two either side of an
exact request and 30fps is 0.033s a frame; it is not there to absorb a wrong composition.
The byte floor is DELIBERATELY LOOSE, and the first version of it was wrong. Set at 4000
bytes per second it refused a real, correct 22-second render, because the videos this skill
generates are type on a flat background and that is exactly what modern codecs compress to
almost nothing. A 22s black-and-type render measures about 57KB. So the floor is not a
quality bar and must never become one: the structural checks (a real container, a video
track with real dimensions, a non-empty mdat or Cluster, the right duration, the right
aspect) do all the actual work, and this only catches the residue case of a file that is
structurally intact and holds essentially no frames. 250 bytes a second means a 22-second
render under about 5.5KB is refused, which no working encoder produces.

why.surface: Built for Instagram Reels: a full-screen, sound-off, scroll-interrupted surface where the video is competing with a thumb already in motion.
why.aspect: 9:16, because you said Reels and Reels is a full-bleed vertical surface. A 16:9 file there gets pillarboxed into a third of the screen and reads as a repost before anyone has watched a frame.
why.seconds: 22 seconds, because that is just under the Reels drop-off cliff. Completion rate is the input the ranking cares about, and a 40-second cut of the same idea completes far less often than a 22-second one.

why.surface: Built for TikTok, where the same clip gets played twice before anyone decides about it, so the cut is timed to survive a loop.
why.aspect: 9:16, because TikTok is vertical-native and crops anything else.
why.seconds: 18 seconds, because TikTok's rewatch loop rewards a cut short enough that the second play starts before anyone decides to leave.

why.surface: Built for YouTube Shorts, where the audience arrived from a search habit rather than a scroll and will hold a beat longer than a Reels viewer.
why.aspect: 9:16, because Shorts only accepts vertical into the Shorts shelf.
why.seconds: 26 seconds, because Shorts tolerates a longer hold than Reels and the extra four seconds buys one more proof shot.

why.surface: Built for the landscape YouTube player, where somebody chose to press play and is not being interrupted by anything.
why.aspect: 16:9, because this is the landscape player and vertical would waste two thirds of the frame.
why.seconds: 45 seconds, because a landscape viewer arrived on purpose and will hold longer than a scroller who was interrupted.

why.surface: Built for the X timeline, where it autoplays muted at thumbnail size inside a column of text and is never tapped to fullscreen.
why.aspect: 1:1, because square holds its size in a timeline that autoplays muted and never gets tapped to fullscreen.
why.seconds: 20 seconds, because a muted autoplay in a feed is judged in the first two and abandoned by thirty.

why.surface: Built for LinkedIn, where the viewer is deciding whether you are credible, not whether you are entertaining.
why.aspect: 1:1, because LinkedIn's feed is square-first and vertical gets cropped in the desktop column.
why.seconds: 30 seconds, because this audience wants the claim substantiated, not teased.

why.surface: Built as a landing page hero loop, which plays behind the headline and the button and must never pull attention off either.
why.aspect: 16:9, because a hero sits behind headline copy and has to span the width of the page.
why.seconds: 12 seconds, because it loops. A hero loop long enough to notice the seam is a hero loop that distracts from the button.

showcase.label: show the thing off
showcase.why: Read as a showcase, so the shape is hook, two proof shots, close. Showing beats explaining: the fastest way to make someone want a thing is to let them watch it work.

demo.label: walk through how it works
demo.why: Read as a demo, so it is a hook and three steps. Three is the most a viewer holds without a scrub bar.

launch.label: announce it
launch.why: Read as a launch, so the claim lands before the proof. An announcement that opens with features has already lost the people who did not know what it was.

ad.label: sell it
ad.why: Read as an ad, so there is a tension beat before the proof. Nothing is worth buying until something is wrong.

teaser.label: make them curious
teaser.why: Read as a teaser, so it withholds. A teaser that shows the product is an ad with less time.

confident.label: confident
confident.why: Confident by default: hard cuts and short fades. Motion that announces itself reads as a template.

energetic.label: energetic
energetic.why: Energetic, so entrances have direction and every beat is shorter than it wants to be.

calm.label: calm
calm.why: Calm, so the fades are long and nothing slides. Restraint is the only way a short video reads as expensive.

technical.label: technical
technical.why: Technical, so the type is monospace-adjacent and the motion stays out of the way. This audience reads the frame.

durationHints.why: You asked for something short, so the platform default was cut to about two thirds.
You asked for depth, so the platform default was stretched by half.

explicitDuration._comment: Matched before anything else. A number the user typed always beats a default.
explicitDuration.why: {seconds} seconds, because you asked for exactly that.
explicitDuration.tooLong: {seconds}s is past the {max}s ceiling in video.json. A render that long is an hour of machine time and almost never what was meant.
explicitDuration.tooShort: {seconds}s is under the {min}s floor in video.json. Nothing legible fits.

aspectOverride._comment: An aspect said out loud always beats the one implied by the platform.

options.why: 9:16, because you asked for vertical outright.
16:9, because you asked for landscape outright.
1:1, because you asked for square outright.
4:5, because you asked for the tall feed crop outright.

_comment: The shot library. Each beat is one entity in the composition, and `jsx` is the literal
source written into the .jsx file with <<tokens>> substituted. Tokens available to every
beat: width height start end sourceIn text subject ink accent background fontWeight
fontSize animIn animOut animDuration index footage logo.
The delimiter is <<angle brackets>> and not {{braces}} because these templates are JSX,
where braces are syntax. A numeric prop must be written `start={<<start>>}`: the braces
belong to the JSX, the angle brackets are the token. Writing `start={{start}}` produces
`start=0`, which is not valid JSX.
Beats are deliberately typographic rather than decorative. The editor's own guidance is that
chrome, scaffolding and ornament draw from a visual budget whose default balance is zero, so
there are no dividers, no eyebrows, no underlines and no boxes here. A cut and a change of
size separate two ideas without any of it.
`weight` is how the duration is split between the beats of a purpose.

hook.label: hook
hook.why: Opens on the subject alone, held large. The first frame is the only one everybody sees, so it carries the whole idea and nothing else.
jsx: animations={[{ type: "<<animIn>>", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }, { type: "<<animOut>>", phase: "out", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }]}

claim.label: claim
claim.why: States the claim once, in the accent colour, so the announcement has a sentence someone could repeat.
jsx: animations={[{ type: "<<animIn>>", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }, { type: "<<animOut>>", phase: "out", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }]}

tension.label: tension
tension.why: One beat of what it was like before. Nothing is worth watching until something is wrong.
jsx: animations={[{ type: "<<animIn>>", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }, { type: "<<animOut>>", phase: "out", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }]}

proof.label: proof
proof.why: The shot that carries the video: real footage of the thing working. Drop a screen recording into `footage` in the spec and it lands here instead of the placeholder.
placeholderJsx: {/* No footage was supplied, so this beat is a hold. Put a screen recording
into the spec's `footage` list and re-run: it lands here as a <video>. */}
animations={[{ type: "<<animIn>>", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }, { type: "<<animOut>>", phase: "out", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }]}

step.label: step
step.why: One numbered step per shot. Numbering is the cheapest way to tell a viewer how much is left.
placeholderJsx: {/* No footage was supplied for this step, so it is set as type. Add a clip
to the spec's `footage` list and it becomes a <video> here. */}
animations={[{ type: "<<animIn>>", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }, { type: "<<animOut>>", phase: "out", duration: "<<animDuration>>" }]}

close.label: close
close.why: Ends on the name, held still. The last frame is the one that gets screenshotted.

logo.label: logo
logo.why: A held logo card at the end, because you asked for one.
placeholderJsx: {/* No logo file in the spec, so the wordmark is set as type. Put a path
into the spec's `logo` field and it becomes an <image> here. */}

_comment: At most one, and only when guessing wrong throws away a whole render. Aspect ratio is the
only decision on this list that cannot be fixed after the fact: a 16:9 file is useless on a
vertical surface, and every other wrong guess (length, tone, wording) is a re-run of a
composition that already exists. So the question fires only when the prompt names no
platform, no aspect, and no purpose that implies one.
question.text: Where is this going? That is the only thing I cannot guess safely, because aspect ratio is the one decision a re-render cannot fix.
question.hint: Answer in one word, or add --assume to take the default.
question.defaultNote: Nothing said where this was going, so it was built for {label} ({aspect}). If that is wrong, say the surface and it re-plans.

_comment: How the thing the video is ABOUT gets pulled out of a sentence. `strip` phrases are removed
from the front and back; whatever survives is the subject. It is deliberately dumb: a
subject that comes out slightly wrong is one word to correct, and a clever extractor that
is confidently wrong is not.
subject.refuseWhy: nothing in that prompt says what the video is ABOUT. Everything else here can be guessed from a default; the subject cannot be invented, and a video about nothing is a wasted render. Say the thing, e.g. "make me a video showing off Toolbay".
subject.why: The subject was read as "{subject}". If that is not the name that should be on screen, say the right one and everything else stays.

_comment: Corrections are not this skill's to store. skills/memory/ already keeps a correction with
the reason it was given, redacts credentials before the write, and can be interrogated and
deleted, so this skill CALLS it and holds nothing of its own. Recalled entries are matched
against the very same match tables above, which is why 'always end on the logo' turns into
the logo beat without anything here knowing that sentence.
_recallQueryWhy: Empty on purpose, and it was 'video' for exactly as long as it took to test. `recall <query>`
scores stored entries against the query text, and the sentence people actually record is
'always end on the logo', which shares no word with 'video' and therefore came back with zero
results while memory was on and the entry was sitting right there. Empty means 'everything in
scope', and relevance is then decided by the match tables above. Set it only if you want the
memory layer's own scoring to pre-filter, and check that corrections still land if you do.
memory.offNote: Memory is off, so nothing you have corrected before is being applied here. Turn it on once with `tb-memory enable` and a correction like "always end on the logo" sticks for every video after it.
memory.unavailableNote: The memory layer could not be reached ({reason}), so this plan is built from video.json alone and no past correction was applied.
memory.appliedNote: Applied because you said so before: "{text}"
memory.recordHint: To make a correction stick: node scripts/tb-video.mjs remember "<what>" --because "<why>"

output._comment: Where the plan, the composition and the render land. Never /tmp; the resolver refuses it.
